text: Look at any real dataset and the columns live on wildly different scales — alcohol content near 13, cholesterol in the hundreds, income in the tens of thousands. Many algorithms treat numbers as numbers, so a column with big values can drown out one with small values, even if the small one is more useful. Feature scaling puts columns on a comparable footing.

Scaling matters when an algorithm compares magnitudes. Distance-based models — k-nearest neighbors, k-means, support vector machines — compute distances between rows, and a feature measured in hundreds contributes far more than one in single digits. Gradient-based and regularized models converge faster when features are on similar scales, which is exactly why we standardized before gradient descent back in Lesson 6. Tree-based models only ask is this value above a threshold, so they don't need scaling at all.

Three common scalers. StandardScaler subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, so each column ends up with mean 0 and standard deviation 1 — the usual default. MinMaxScaler squeezes each column into the range 0 to 1 — good for a bounded range, but sensitive to outliers. RobustScaler subtracts the median and divides by the interquartile range, so extreme values barely influence the scale.

scikit-learn's bundled wine dataset has 178 wines with 13 chemical measurements. Alcohol ranges from 11 to 14.8, malic acid from 0.7 to 5.8, but proline ranges from 278 all the way to 1,680 — varying by over a thousand, while alcohol varies by just a few units. In a distance calculation, proline would decide almost everything.

A scaler learns statistics from data, so the same rule from Lesson 8 applies — split first, fit on the training set only, then transform both sets with those training statistics. The training columns end up with mean exactly zero, as designed. The test columns don't, and shouldn't — they're measured with the training yardstick, just like new production data will be.

Comparing a k-nearest-neighbors classifier and a decision tree, both on raw and on scaled features: scaling took kNN from 72.2 percent to 96.3 percent on the exact same test wines. The decision tree, which ignores magnitudes entirely, scored identically either way, 94.4 percent.

The boxplots make it visual — on the raw data, proline dwarfs everything else; after standardizing, all four columns share a common scale. Now, choosing a scaler with outliers in play: six values where one is a wild outlier, 300, against five ordinary values clustered around 10 to 13.

With standard and min-max scaling, the five ordinary values get crushed into a tiny sliver because the outlier stretched the whole scale. Robust scaling keeps the ordinary values well spread out, from negative 1.0 to 0.6, and simply lets the outlier stay large on its own.

So default to standardization, use min-max when you need a bounded range, and use robust scaling when outliers are present and you've chosen to keep them. To recap: scale for distance-based, gradient-based, and regularized models, skip it for trees, and always fit scalers on training data only. Next up, lesson 11: creating new features.
